impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's Penumbra framework—which dispenses with Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis for determining a reference patent's prior art date under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2)—is correct, or whether a reference patent can claim the filing date of its provisional application only if at least one claim is supported by the provisional's written description.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's final written decision finding claims of the '409 patent unpatentable as obvious, holding that the Board needed to reconsider whether a key prior art reference (Carrier) was entitled to its provisional application filing date under AIA § 102(d)(2). The court questioned the Board's Penumbra framework, which had relaxed the written description requirements for establishing prior art dates. This decision could significantly affect which references qualify as prior art in IPR proceedings under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a more rigorous standard for establishing prior art dates of reference patents, potentially shielding patents from invalidation based on references that cannot demonstrate full written description support in their provisional applications.
impacts.negativeImplications: Petitioners in IPR proceedings face greater difficulty establishing earlier prior art dates for reference patents, potentially increasing the cost and complexity of patent challenges.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court may assess copyright infringement damages via a hypothetical negotiation rather than deferring to the terms of an existing license agreement, and what constitutes permissible use of the 'book of wisdom' in calculating such damages against the government.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to use a hypothetical negotiation to assess copyright infringement damages for the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA® software, rather than relying on the existing license agreement's terms. However, the court vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. This case provides important guidance on copyright damages methodology in government contract disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's endorsement of the hypothetical negotiation framework, which can yield higher damages than rigid adherence to existing license terms when the government exceeds its license.
impacts.negativeImplications: The court's limitation on the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and prohibition of non-compensatory damages constrains the recovery available to copyright holders, particularly in government infringement cases.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a dispute over Ford's development of competing software after licensing Versata's automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment on trade secret damages and remanded for a new trial, instructing the court to consider two damages models it had previously rejected. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages, reinstating the jury award. Importantly, the court affirmed the finding of trade secret misappropriation liability against Ford for developing competing software (PDO) while licensing Versata's ACM and MCA software. This case has significant implications for software licensing relationships and trade secret protection.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors gain stronger protection against licensees who develop competing products using knowledge gained during the licensing relationship, with broader damages models potentially available at trial.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that license software and later develop competing in-house solutions face heightened trade secret misappropriation liability, even when license agreements expire, creating risk for technology transition strategies.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents to the licensee, entitling the licensee to sue for infringement in its own name without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee had ceased business operations triggering automatic termination of the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the exclusive license agreement between Texas A&M University and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights in the licensed patents, making TexasLDPC tantamount to a patent owner with standing to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC had not ceased business operations merely by shifting to patent enforcement activities. This decision clarifies the standard for when an exclusive licensee has sufficient rights to maintain an infringement suit independently.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees, including patent assertion entities, benefit from a clearer path to maintaining infringement suits without joining university or other patent owners, reducing procedural obstacles to enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on challenging the standing of exclusive licensees, particularly those whose primary business activity is patent enforcement rather than product development.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination, or whether the dispute is a state law contract matter for the regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute between T-Mobile and KAIFI about whether T-Mobile owed a contingent payment under a settlement agreement conditioned on whether any 'Asserted Claim survives the EPR.' The court determined the dispute was fundamentally one of contract interpretation under Texas law that did not necessarily require resolution of a substantial patent law question, and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision narrows the scope of Federal Circuit jurisdiction over patent settlement disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements may benefit from having contract interpretation disputes heard in regional circuits, which may be more experienced with general contract law principles.
impacts.negativeImplications: The jurisdictional uncertainty created by this ruling may complicate settlement negotiations and dispute resolution planning, as parties cannot assume the Federal Circuit will resolve disputes arising from patent-related settlement terms.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellation designs for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's damages analysis and infringement finding were legally sufficient.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents (relating to non-uniform constellations for communication systems) while affirming eligibility for the '509 and '922 patent claims. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. The distinction turned on whether the claims were directed to abstract mathematical optimization or to specific technological implementations. This case provides important guidance on Section 101 eligibility for communications technology patents embedded in industry standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technological implementations rather than abstract optimization benefit from affirmed eligibility, particularly in the standards-essential patent context where damages models were upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement risk for standards-essential patents, and the split eligibility ruling creates uncertainty about the scope of patent protection for constellation design innovations.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's design patent infringement framework under Egyptian Goddess improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction involving functionality questions in design patents should be decided by a jury rather than the court.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied rehearing en banc on design patent infringement standards, with significant dissents. The majority held that the Egyptian Goddess framework properly allows courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment by assessing both similarities and differences. Chief Judge Moore, joined by Judge Reyna, dissented, arguing the current approach improperly shifts focus to dissimilarity and allows courts to usurp jury functions on factual functionality questions. Judges Stoll and Stark also dissented without opinion. This fractured decision signals ongoing tension within the court on design patent infringement standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the maintained ability to obtain summary judgment on design patent non-infringement where visual differences are sufficiently distinct, preserving a cost-effective defense strategy.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued risk that courts will grant summary judgment based on differences without full jury consideration, and the strong dissents signal potential instability in the current framework that creates litigation uncertainty.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in the weight-to-weight ratio limitation to refer to freebase forms rather than salt forms, and whether a bond pending appeal was properly waived under Rule 65(c).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction preventing Hetero Labs from launching a generic version of Nuedexta (used for treating pseudobulbar affect) based on likely infringement of the '282 patent, but vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement. The claim construction ruling on whether drug compound terms refer to freebase or salt forms has significant implications for pharmaceutical patent scope. The bond ruling reinforces that preliminary injunctions in Hatch-Waxman cases require security pending appeal.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmed preliminary injunction framework and the favorable claim construction that broadens patent protection for drug combination patents, helping prevent generic competition before patent expiry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face barriers to market entry when branded companies obtain preliminary injunctions, and the bond requirement vacatur may impose additional financial obligations on branded companies seeking injunctive relief.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of patents claiming drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implant compositions used in drug-eluting coronary stents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict finding infringement and no invalidity, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL of invalidity for anticipation and JMOL of non-infringement of the '296 patent covering drug-releasing biodegradable polymer fiber compositions used in coronary stents. The court found the prior art anticipated the asserted claims and that BSC's products did not infringe. This decision eliminates a significant patent liability for BSC in the medical device space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device companies benefit from the reversal of infringement liability, reinforcing that prior art disclosures of similar polymer-drug compositions can invalidate composition claims and narrowing the scope of university patent enforcement in the medical device sector.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and technology transfer offices face a setback in enforcing composition patents against major medical device manufacturers, as the court's anticipation and non-infringement findings narrow available patent protection for incremental innovations.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the asserted claims of patents covering crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate salts, pharmaceutical formulations, and methods of cancer treatment have adequate written description support under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's patents covering cabozantinib malate (the active ingredient in Cabometyx® for treating kidney, liver, and thyroid cancer) have adequate written description, rejecting MSN's invalidity challenge. The court upheld the patents' validity, which protects Exelixis's blockbuster cancer drug through 2030. This decision preserves significant branded pharmaceutical exclusivity in the oncology space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of written description adequacy for crystalline form and salt patents, reinforcing patent protection strategies for commercially important drug polymorphs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers face continued exclusion from the cabozantinib market, and the ruling makes it harder to challenge written description support for crystalline form patents covering known API salt forms.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations under 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for Tucker Act claims against the government is subject to American Pipe tolling, and whether Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of claims by a bank holding company and its subsidiaries arising from the 2008 financial crisis and government conservatorship of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. The court recognized that its prior decision in Bright v. United States had been implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's ANZ Securities decision, which held that statutes of repose (and analogous non-tolling limitations periods) are not subject to American Pipe class action tolling.
impacts.negativeImplications: Financial institutions and investors with claims against the government arising from the 2008 financial crisis lose the ability to rely on American Pipe tolling to extend filing deadlines, effectively barring claims that were not individually filed within the six-year limitations period. This ruling also broadly limits tolling for Tucker Act claims.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulatory 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on such a deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade's declaration that Commerce's 15-day participation deadline in antidumping sunset reviews was void. The court held that the statute is silent on when domestic interested parties must express willingness to participate, and Commerce's regulatory deadline was a permissible exercise of delegated authority and the product of reasoned decisionmaking. This decision preserves Commerce's ability to efficiently administer sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders, which directly affect import competition.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers seeking to maintain antidumping protections benefit from clear procedural rules, and Commerce retains administrative flexibility to manage sunset reviews efficiently through reasonable regulatory deadlines.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic interested parties who miss the 15-day filing deadline risk losing antidumping protections, as the court validated Commerce's strict procedural requirements that can result in revocation of antidumping duty orders.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce properly determined that government-directed debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit to a foreign steel manufacturer, and what methodology applies when private investor prices exist for evaluating equity infusions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and reinstated Commerce's original determination that three debt-to-equity conversions performed by the Korean government conferred countervailable benefits on Dongbu Steel. The court rejected Commerce's later determinations (submitted under protest after remands) that found no benefit, holding that Commerce's original methodology was correct. This decision reinforces the enforcement of countervailing duty laws against foreign government subsidies to steel manufacturers through equity infusions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and manufacturers benefit from stronger enforcement of countervailing duty laws, as the decision supports finding countervailable benefits in government-directed debt-to-equity conversions that distort international trade competition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers receiving government equity infusions face increased risk of countervailing duties on U.S. imports, potentially affecting pricing strategies and market access for subsidized foreign competitors.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on Section 101 eligibility grounds after already concluding that venue is improper and dismissing on that basis.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds, holding that a court may address and rule on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion for patent ineligibility even after determining that venue is improper under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b). The '979 patent claims relating to e-commerce 'bridge computer' methods were found ineligible under Section 101. This decision confirms that courts can issue merits rulings on patent eligibility alongside venue dismissals, providing defendants with preclusive effect.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain Section 101 eligibility rulings even when venue is improper, potentially precluding re-filing of the same claims in a proper venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk of receiving adverse eligibility rulings in venues where they have no opportunity to litigate fully, as courts may adjudicate patent eligibility even when dismissing for improper venue.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly awarded attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctioned plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 for filing a meritless patent infringement complaint and attempting to amend after agreeing not to do so.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal with prejudice, the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen under Section 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel for filing a frivolous patent infringement suit regarding electrically controlled spectacles. The court found the case 'exceptional' warranting fees and upheld sanctions for counsel's conduct in seeking to amend after agreeing not to. This decision reinforces deterrence against meritless patent assertions and strengthens fee-shifting consequences.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from robust fee-shifting and sanctions mechanisms that deter frivolous patent infringement suits, reducing litigation costs from meritless claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face significant financial exposure for pursuing aggressive enforcement strategies, as courts may impose both Section 285 fees and personal sanctions on counsel for filing insufficiently supported claims.
